vignette: Leila, a 51-year-old social ministry worker of Middle Eastern descent, had always been driven to help others. Her work at a local community center was more than just a job - it was her calling. However, the past few months had seen Leila struggling to maintain her usual enthusiasm and dedication. She found herself constantly on edge, her irritability simmering just below the surface. The slightest provocation could set off an angry outburst, leaving her feeling ashamed and worried about losing control. This wasn't the first time Leila's emotions had gotten the better of her. As a child, she had endured physical abuse at the hands of her caregiver, an experience that still lingered in her mind like an open wound. When memories of those events surfaced, Leila would involuntarily tense up, her body assuming the same defensive posture it had all those years ago. She couldn't quite put into words what had happened - the experiences remained stubbornly nonverbal, locked away in a part of her mind that she dare not explore. Lately, however, these memories had begun to resurface with increasing frequency. When they did, Leila would feel an intense rage building inside her, threatening to spill over at any moment. She started to avoid situations that might trigger these recollections - like going to work or study, where the proximity of others made her feel trapped and vulnerable. Instead, she found herself gravitating towards exits, positioning herself near doors or corridors so that she could make a quick escape if needed. As time went on, Leila's avoidance behaviors began to have a tangible impact on her daily life. She stopped attending community meetings, citing scheduling conflicts or family emergencies as excuses. Her colleagues noticed the change in her and began to comment on it - not unkindly, but with concern. Leila knew that she was isolating herself, but the prospect of being alone with another person, even someone she trusted, filled her with a creeping sense of dread. This dread manifested itself in strange ways. She would find herself constantly scanning her surroundings, checking behind her to see if anyone was following. It wasn't just people - Leila became hyper-vigilant about potential dangers lurking in every corner of her world. She began to overreact to minor setbacks or unexpected noises, leaping into a state of high alert as if her life depended on it. Despite these growing difficulties, Leila continued to function, albeit at a reduced capacity. Her work suffered, and she knew that something had to give. It was only when she found herself lashing out at a client - someone she had been trying to help, no less - that Leila realized the full extent of her problem. She couldn't keep living like this, perpetually walking on eggshells, waiting for the next shoe to drop. The incident with the client marked a turning point for Leila. Ashamed and worried about what might happen if she lost control again, she began to seek help. Her biggest fear was losing herself completely - becoming so consumed by her own rage and anxiety that she would cease to be the compassionate person she once was. As she sat in her therapist's office, preparing to confront the demons of her past, Leila couldn't shake the feeling that she was standing at a crossroads. She could continue down the path of avoidance and isolation or take a tentative step forward, into the unknown.
